label: Reference aid; the AHJ and the printed NEC govern.

sections.title: Article 600 — Electric Signs and Outline Lighting
sections.plain_explanation:
This article covers signs, outline lighting, and skeleton tubing — the lighted advertising and identification equipment on commercial buildings. Its field core is simple: a proper sign branch circuit and a real disconnect at the sign.

The numbers that size a sign job:
• Sign branch circuit — 20A minimum, serving signs and outline lighting only (600.5)
• Pedestrian entrances — at least one outlet in an accessible location at each entrance to each tenant space, for sign or outline-lighting use, supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that supplies no other load (600.5(A)); service hallways and corridors are not considered accessible to pedestrians. of a commercial building or occupancy accessible to pedestrians, supplied by that 20A sign circuit (600.5(A))
• Load calculations — each required sign branch circuit is figured at not less than 1,200 VA in feeder and service calculations (220.14(F))
• Neon and skeleton tubing — the high-voltage secondary wiring follows its own part of this article (600.31 and 600.32), and the tubing and its power supplies are listed equipment, not field-fabricated parts 600.5(B): circuits supplying signs with incandescent and fluorescent sources are rated 20A maximum; neon transformer or power-supply circuits are rated 30A maximum. Each sign needs a disconnect per 600.6.
sections.on_the_job: If a bid has signage, price the circuit and the disconnect, not just the sign.
sections.figure_idea: Storefront with a channel-letter sign fed from its own labeled circuit.

sections.title: Sign branch circuits — 20A, signs only
sections.plain_explanation:
600.5(A) requires at least one receptacle outlet in an accessible location at EACH ENTRANCE of each commercial building or occupancy that is accessible to pedestrians, supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that serves no other load. The sign circuit itself is the same family of rule: a sign or outline lighting system is supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that serves no other loads, other than signs and outline lighting tied to the same work.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 600.5: The sign circuit can now also feed equipment that controls the sign, and the delivery-door and service-corridor exemption became a formal exception. The dedicated sign circuit can now also carry loads that control the sign, such as a time clock or photocell (Exception No. 2).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Don't hang storefront lighting or receptacles on the sign circuit.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 already sets a 20A minimum on commercial branch circuits — the code and company practice land in the same place here.
sections.figure_idea: Storefront sign on its own labeled 20A circuit.

sections.title: Sign disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation: The conductors feeding a sign, outline lighting system, or skeleton tubing are controlled by an externally operable switch or breaker that opens all ungrounded conductors. The disconnect sits where the circuit enters the sign enclosure, body, or pole; the 2020 rules in 600.6(A) also cover within-sight, lockable, and remote-location marking situations so service people and first responders can find and kill it.
sections.on_the_job: Stand at the sign — can you see and reach its disconnect? If it's remote, it must be marked at the sign.
sections.figure_idea: Sign disconnect at the point of entry into the sign body, placard for a remote disconnect beside it.

sections.title: Retrofit kits (new in 2020)
sections.plain_explanation:
Converting an existing sign to new lighting technology is a listed-kit job, not a lamp swap. A general-use or sign-specific retrofit kit must be listed and labeled and must include installation instructions for field conversion of the host sign. The kit is installed per those instructions; wiring methods follow Chapter 3 (with the Class 2 path in 600.12(C), 600.24, and 600.33); parts not replaced are inspected and damaged parts are repaired or replaced; workmanship follows 110.12; and the retrofitted sign is marked per 600.4(B) — including the alert label where tubular LED lamps run on the existing sign sockets, so nobody later installs fluorescent lamps. The 600.2 retrofit definitions (host sign, subassembly, general-use and sign-specific kits) ride with this section.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 600.35: Section 600.35 had redundant requirements removed, which are already covered in Chapters 1-4 of NEC.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Before quoting an LED sign conversion, confirm the kit is listed for that host sign and plan the label — an inspector can fail an unlisted conversion even if it lights.

sections.title: Article 604 — Manufactured Wiring Systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Intro: factory-built wiring assemblies — plug-together branch-circuit and feeder components — used heavily in office fit-outs. The components must be listed and used as a system, not mixed and matched between manufacturers.

Where Sharma meets it: relocatable wiring for office partitions, pre-wired workstation feeds, and raised-access-floor whips on tenant fit-outs. The connectors are keyed to the system — a whip that will not mate is the system telling you the parts came from different manufacturers, and forcing the connection voids the listing. Home runs land in the panel like any other branch circuit; the manufactured part is only the distribution between the connection point and the outlets, and every run is installed so it can be inspected and reconfigured without disturbing the building wiring.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma hits these on tenant work; keep one manufacturer's system end to end and follow its instructions.

sections.title: Article 605 — Office Furnishings
sections.plain_explanation:
Intro: electrical rules for wired office partitions and furniture systems — how powered furniture connects to the building wiring, and the limits on cord connections and interconnecting partitions.

The connection points that matter: powered furnishings connect to the building wiring at the fixed connection point the system is listed for — never by a cord pushed through a wall or ceiling — and freestanding partitions interconnect only with the manufacturer's listed connectors, in the combinations and circuit counts the listing allows. The furniture vendor's shop drawings are an electrical document on these jobs: they show where the building feed lands, and they belong in the job file before rough-in, not in the furniture installer's truck at trim.
sections.on_the_job: Coordinate furniture power early on office jobs; the furniture system is listed equipment, not field-built wiring.

sections.title: Article 610 — Cranes and Hoists
sections.plain_explanation:
Intro: wiring, disconnects, and controls for cranes and hoists — runway conductors, festoon wiring, and the disconnecting means that let a crane be locked out for service. Rare in Sharma's current work; recognize it and price from the article when a warehouse job includes one.

The working parts when one does appear: the runway contact conductors have their own disconnecting means, lockable in the open position, so the whole runway can be made dead for service; the crane itself carries a disconnect for its driving machinery; and conductor sizing follows this article's duty-based approach for the crane's combined motor loads rather than a straight 430 feeder calculation. Festoon and pendant wiring is supported so strain never lands on the terminations — a crane that travels beats on its wiring every cycle.
sections.on_the_job: On a warehouse bid, find the crane's disconnect and runway-conductor scope in the drawings before pricing. If the crane package is by others, say so in the bid notes — otherwise the runway disconnect and the lockout point land on Sharma by default.

sections.title: Article 620 — Elevators, Dumbwaiters, Escalators, Moving Walks, Platform Lifts, and Stairway Chairlifts
sections.plain_explanation:
This article covers the electrical installation for elevators and similar equipment: the machine-room disconnect, the branch circuits that serve the car and the machine space, GFCI protection in pits and hoistways, and selective coordination where several machines share a feeder. Elevator work is always coordinated with the elevator contractor and ASME A17.1 — the electrical scope is defined here, the machine scope is theirs.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 620.36: Received substantiation specifies which cable types may be installed in elevator raceway or traveling cable. Shielded pair cables, coaxial cables, and communication cables complying with 800.179 are now specifically permitted in Section 620.36. 620.Sl(A) Type. Ex. No.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On a job with an elevator, Sharma's piece is typically the disconnect, the car and machine-room circuits, and pit/hoistway receptacles — confirm that split in the bid, not on site.
sections.figure_idea: Machine room: one labeled disconnect per unit, car circuits tapped ahead of it.

sections.title: GFCI protection in elevator spaces
sections.plain_explanation: All 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles installed in pits, in hoistways, on elevator and dumbwaiter cars, in escalator and moving-walk wellways, and in the runways and machinery spaces of platform lifts and stairway chairlifts must be of the GFCI type — the protection is at the receptacle, not just a GFCI breaker upstream. Receptacles in machine rooms, control rooms, machinery spaces, and control spaces must also have GFCI protection for personnel. A permanently installed sump pump in the pit must be permanently wired or supplied by a single GFCI-protected receptacle — the blanket sump-pump exemption as printed in the 2017 edition is gone in 2020.
sections.on_the_job: Use GFCI receptacles (not a breaker alone) at pit and hoistway locations, and don't assume a pit sump pump is exempt. The 2020 Handbook notes the hard-wired sump-pump wording sits awkwardly with 422.5(A)(6) — a point flagged for Mike and worth an AHJ conversation on a real job.
sections.figure_idea: Pit receptacle with the GFCI device at the outlet, sump pump on a single protected receptacle.

sections.title: Car lighting, receptacle, ventilation, heating and air-conditioning branch circuits
sections.plain_explanation: This section puts the car loads on their own dedicated circuits, apart from the driving-machine supply. Under 620.22(A), a separate branch circuit supplies the car lights, receptacle(s), auxiliary lighting power source, and ventilation on each car, and the required car lighting must not be connected to the load side of a GFCI — a tripped service receptacle must not black out the car. Under 620.22(B), car heating and air-conditioning units are supplied by their own separate branch circuit. The overcurrent device protecting each circuit is located in the machine room or control space for that car, and neither circuit is opened by the driving-machine disconnect (620.51), so the car stays lit and ventilated while the machine is locked out for service.
sections.on_the_job: Two dedicated car circuits, not one: lights, receptacles, and ventilation on the first; car heat and AC on their own. Both breakers live in the machine room or control space — not in the car and not on the machine disconnect.

sections.title: Disconnecting means — one per unit, lockable open only
sections.plain_explanation: Each elevator, dumbwaiter, escalator, moving walk, platform lift, or stairway chairlift gets its own disconnecting means: an enclosed, externally operable fused motor-circuit switch or circuit breaker that disconnects the driving machine. Two details are exam-and-inspection favorites: the disconnect must be lockable in the open position only — it is not permitted to be lockable in the closed position — and it must not disconnect the car lighting, receptacle, and ventilation circuits covered by 620.22, 620.23, and 620.24, which are arranged to stay energized for service work in the car.
sections.on_the_job: One disconnect per unit, labeled, and never let it kill the car light circuit — a serviceman in a dark car is exactly what the rule prevents.
sections.figure_idea: Machine-room disconnect with lock hasp in the open position only; car-light circuit breaker in a separate enclosure.

sections.title: Selective coordination
sections.plain_explanation: Where more than one driving machine disconnecting means is supplied by a single feeder, the overcurrent devices in each disconnect must be selectively coordinated with any other supply-side overcurrent devices, so one fault doesn't strand every car on the feeder. The coordination must be selected by a licensed professional engineer or other qualified person engaged primarily in the design, installation, or maintenance of electrical systems, and the selection — including device settings, a documentation point the 2020 edition added — must be documented and made available to those authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain, and operate the system. Enclosures containing coordinated devices are marked per 620.65.
sections.on_the_job: Multi-elevator jobs: coordination is an engineering deliverable, not a field decision. Get the documented study before trim-out.
sections.figure_idea: Two elevator disconnects on one feeder with the coordination study folder in the machine room.

sections.title: Article 625 — Electric Vehicle Power Transfer System
sections.plain_explanation:
The 2020 edition renamed this article from 'Charging System' to 'Power Transfer System' because the equipment now moves power both ways — charging, power export, and bidirectional flow are all inside the article's scope. The field core for Sharma: a dedicated branch circuit per outlet (625.40), protection at 125% of a continuous load (625.41, 625.42), a lockable disconnect above the threshold (625.43), and GFCI on every charging receptacle (625.54).

One more field number: the EVSE output cable (to the vehicle) is limited to 25 ft of overall usable length unless the listed equipment includes a cable management system (625.17(B)(3)); power-supply cords on cord-and-plug EVSE have their own length limits. A longer cord draped across a garage floor or a parking space is a trip hazard and a listing problem at the same time — plan the charger location so 25 ft reaches the charge port of the vehicles the space serves.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 625.6: Clarified which electric vehicle equipment involved in electric vehicle power transfer systems should be listed in Section 625.6.
• 625.49: Created a new Section 625.49 stating that electric vehicle power export equipment (EVPE) and bidirectional electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) are permitted to be a part of interconnected power systems operating in an island mode condition.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Garage EV points follow Sharma's garage rules (S-07, S-01) only where they don't conflict with Article 625 — the article wins where they differ.

The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020.

sections.title: Electric vehicle branch circuit — one outlet, one circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
Each outlet installed for the purpose of charging electric vehicles must be supplied by an individual branch circuit, and each such circuit must have no other outlets. In the 2020 text that rule applies to every EV outlet regardless of size — the 'greater than 16A or 120V' qualifier and the exception letting one branch circuit feed multiple chargers are 2023 changes that apply in Florida only to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.).

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 625.40: Only EV charging outlets rated over 16 amps or 120 volts now need an individual branch circuit, and a new exception allows several chargers on one circuit when the load is managed. An individual branch circuit is now required only for outlets serving EV supply equipment (EVSE) rated more than 16 amps or more than 120 volts.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Two cars means two circuits under Florida's 2020 rules. Power sharing between chargers happens upstream through load management (625.42), not by doubling up a branch circuit.
sections.figure_idea: Two garage EV outlets, each home-run to its own breaker.

The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection — 125% of maximum load
sections.plain_explanation:
EV charging is a continuous load — a charger can pull its full rating for three hours or more on an overnight charge. So the overcurrent device protecting a feeder or branch circuit that supplies EV charging is sized at not less than 125% of the equipment's maximum load, and the conductors are sized to the same figure (625.42).
• 32 A charger → 125% is 40 A → a 40 A breaker.
• 40 A charger → 125% is 50 A → a 50 A breaker.
• 48 A charger → 125% is 60 A → a 60 A breaker.
Size from the charger's maximum setting, not from the car plugged in today and not from a lower setting picked in an app. Where access to the adjustment is restricted, or a listed load management system caps the load, 625.42 lets the service and feeder be figured at the capped load — but each EV outlet still gets its own branch circuit (625.40).
sections.on_the_job: Two-car garage in Orlando on a 200 A Siemens panel. One side is a plug-in charger set to 40 A on a 240 V receptacle: 40 × 1.25 = 50, so it lands on a 50 A two-pole GFCI breaker — 625.54 requires GFCI protection for the charging receptacle — with 8 AWG copper, good for 50 A at 75 °C. The other side is a hardwired unit set to 48 A: 48 × 1.25 = 60, a 60 A breaker, and the wire steps up to 6 AWG copper because 8 AWG stops at 50 A. The panel schedule is written from the chargers' maximum settings, not from the two cars that happen to live there now.
sections.figure_idea: Breaker schedule callout: 48A EVSE → 60A breaker, conductor sized to match.
sections.why_it_exists: A breaker and its conductors sized at exactly 100% of a load that runs all night sit at their thermal edge for hours at a time. Breakers trip on heat, terminations loosen and cook over repeated long cycles, and insulation ages fast when it runs hot. The 125% factor is the Code's continuous-load margin: it keeps the device, the lugs and the wire in their comfortable range for the whole charge, every night, for years.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing from the setting on the screen: 'the charger is set to 32 A, so a 40 A breaker is plenty' — until the owner raises it to 48 A in the app and the 40 A breaker cooks every night. Unless the adjustment is restricted the way 625.42 requires, the maximum load is the equipment's maximum setting. The other trap is a 48 A charger on a 50 A breaker because a 50 A receptacle was handy: 50 is less than 60, and the math fails before the receptacle question even starts.

sections.title: Rating — charging is a continuous load; load management
sections.plain_explanation:
Electric vehicle charging loads are considered continuous loads for this article — that is the root of the 125% sizing in 625.41. Where a listed automatic load management system is used, the maximum equipment load on a service or feeder is the maximum load the system permits: the managed cap, not the sum of every charger's nameplate, is the figure used for the service and feeder. Adjustable equipment is figured at its setting only where the adjustment means meets the section's conditions.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 625.42: The two ways to size services and feeders below the nameplate, load management and restricted adjustable settings, now sit in 625.42(A) and (B) and tie to the energy management rules in 750.30. Every EV charger counts as a continuous load, so size its circuit conductors and overcurrent device at 125 percent of the rating.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Load management is how a 100A or 200A service legally carries two chargers — but it changes the service calculation, never the per-outlet branch-circuit rule in 625.40.

sections.title: Disconnecting means — over 60A or 150V to ground
sections.plain_explanation:
EV charging equipment rated more than 60A, or more than 150V to ground, must have a disconnecting means that is readily accessible and capable of being locked in the open position, with the locking provision remaining in place as 110.25 requires. Equipment at or under both thresholds does not need the separate disconnect under this section.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 625.43: When the disconnect for larger EV equipment (over 60 amps, or more than 150 volts to ground) is remote, the equipment now needs a plaque telling where it is. New: if the disconnect sits away from the EVSE or wireless power transfer equipment (WPTE), a plaque on that equipment must show its location.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Big commercial chargers and DC fast-charge equipment cross the threshold — plan the disconnect location at rough-in, not at the final.
sections.figure_idea: Wall-mounted lockable disconnect beside a high-output charger.

sections.title: Equipment connections — how the charger plugs in
sections.plain_explanation:
625.44 sorts electric vehicle equipment by how it connects to the premises wiring, and each style carries its own connection rule. Portable equipment connects cord-and-plug through a receptacle. Stationary equipment may also be cord-and-plug connected where the section permits it, and fastened-in-place equipment has its own provisions, including direct wiring. Where a receptacle is the connection, it must be a listed receptacle of the rating and configuration the equipment requires — the charger nameplate, not habit, picks the receptacle. The dwelling case crews see most is a 240-volt receptacle feeding a plug-in charger: the receptacle rating, the branch-circuit rating, and the charger's continuous draw all have to agree, which is why this section is read together with 625.41 and 625.42.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 625.44(A): Received substantiation that led to the addition of 60-ampere receptacles to the list of permitted receptacle amperages for portable electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) in Section 625.44(A).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Plug-in charger on a 50 A receptacle: the circuit is sized for the continuous load at 125 percent (a 40 A charger on a 50 A circuit), the receptacle matches the circuit, and the equipment is the listed unit the homeowner bought — not a dryer receptacle borrowed for the garage. If the charger is hard-wired instead, 625.44 steps aside and the disconnect rules of 625.43 decide.

sections.title: Connector storage — 18 in. indoors, 24 in. outdoors
sections.plain_explanation:
Unless the equipment is listed and marked for a different arrangement, the coupling means — the vehicle connector — must be stored or located at a height of:
• Not less than 18 in. above the floor for indoor locations.
• Not less than 24 in. above grade for outdoor locations.
It also has to be positioned so it can couple directly to the vehicle: stored where the cord actually reaches the charge port, not coiled on a hook across the garage. The heights are minimums, and they are measured to where the connector sits in its holster or storage position.
sections.on_the_job: Florida makes this one easy to get wrong. A wall charger inside a garage gets its holster mounted so the connector docks at 18 in. or more above the slab — above the water line when the floor is hosed out or a storm blows rain under the door. The same charger on an outside wall or a carport post is an outdoor location: 24 in. minimum above grade, because an afternoon storm can pond water against that wall in minutes. Measure to where the connector actually sits docked, not to the top of the holster bracket.
sections.figure_idea: Connector docked in its holster at compliant height, indoor and outdoor versions.
sections.why_it_exists: A connector stored down at floor level lives in the worst spot in the building: garage floor water, driveway runoff, tire paths and dropped tools. Water and grit in the connector contacts corrode them, and a damaged connector can damage the vehicle's inlet too. The minimum heights keep the coupling means out of standing water and out from under tires.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is carrying the indoor number outside: 18 in. is the indoor floor measurement. Outdoors the minimum is 24 in., measured from grade — not from the driveway's high spot or the top of a paver. The second trap is measuring to the holster's mounting screws instead of to the stored connector itself; the rule is about where the coupling means sits.

sections.title: Ventilation — only where the listing requires it
sections.plain_explanation:
Indoor EV charging needs mechanical ventilation only where the listing says so:
• Equipment listed as requiring ventilation for indoor use: mechanical ventilation is required.
• Equipment listed for indoor charging without ventilation: none is required — most modern residential EVSE is listed this way.
• Where ventilation is required, it is a permanent system: supply air and exhaust, vented directly to the outdoors, arranged for the vehicles being charged.
The listing and the installation instructions are the rule here — equipment is installed per its listing (110.3(B)), and 625.52 keys the ventilation question to that listing.
sections.on_the_job: Garage install in a Florida home: a 48 A wall-mounted EVSE on a 60 A circuit (625.41) — the nameplate and instructions say listed for indoor use, no ventilation required. The crew prices no ductwork, and notes the listing line on the work order so the inspector sees the basis at rough-in. Across town, a fleet shop buys chargers whose listing requires ventilation for indoor use: that job carries a permanent supply-and-exhaust system vented straight outdoors, priced before the chargers are mounted.

sections.why_it_exists: Some charging equipment and battery chemistries can give off gases while charging, and in a closed garage those gases must not be allowed to build up. Equipment listed for indoor use without ventilation has that hazard engineered out, so the Code does not make every garage charger carry ductwork it does not need — the ventilation follows the listing, not a blanket rule.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the blanket answer — every indoor EV charger needs mechanical ventilation. 625.52 requires ventilation only where the equipment is listed as requiring it for indoor use. The reverse trap also fails jobs: skipping ventilation where the listing does require it, or offering a portable fan where a permanent supply-and-exhaust system vented outdoors is required.

sections.title: GFCI protection for personnel — every EV receptacle
sections.plain_explanation: All receptacles installed for the connection of electric vehicle charging must be provided with GFCI protection for personnel. The requirement is in addition to the dwelling garage rules in 210.8 — a 240V charging receptacle is not exempt, and indoor locations are not exempt. The charger receptacle is the outlet being protected; the EVSE's own internal personnel protection system does not substitute for it.
sections.on_the_job: Treat every EV receptacle as a GFCI point, 120V or 240V, indoor or out.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: S-07's dual-function point is a 120V device. A 240V EV circuit is not an S-07 point — meet 625.54 with the listed protection method specified for the job (Mike/Sanjay decide the device per job), and never describe a 240V charger circuit as a DFN point.

sections.title: Wet location — weatherproof enclosure
sections.plain_explanation:
625.56 is one sentence long: receptacles installed outdoors or in wet locations for EV charging must be enclosed so the enclosure is weatherproof with the attachment plug cap inserted or removed. In plain terms, weatherproof while in use — the same duty other outdoor receptacles carry under 406.9(B)(1).
• A standard flip cover is weatherproof only with nothing plugged in. It fails this rule the moment a charge cord is connected.
• The cover that passes is an in-use ('bubble') cover: a deep hood that closes over the plug and cord for the whole charge.
• The receptacle still owes GFCI protection for personnel under 625.54. The cover and the GFCI are separate duties — one does not excuse the other.
sections.on_the_job: Florida spec home with the charger receptacle on the driveway wall: a 240 V, 50 A receptacle on GFCI protection (625.54) with a bubble cover over it, so the EVSE plug stays dry through an afternoon thunderstorm in the middle of a charge. Sharma standard: put the in-use cover on the rough-in material list for every outdoor charger receptacle — standard flip covers don't meet in-use duty, and swapping a cover after final is a callback, not a change order.

sections.why_it_exists: An outdoor EV receptacle stays plugged in for hours, usually unattended and often overnight, through Florida rain. A cover that only works with nothing plugged in protects the receptacle exactly when it is not being used. Water tracking into a live receptacle corrodes the contacts, builds leakage paths and can energize the enclosure — the in-use cover keeps the weather out for the entire charge.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'weatherproof means a flip cover.' A flip cover is weatherproof with the plug removed; 625.56 requires weatherproof with the plug inserted OR removed. The other wrong answer is that the EVSE's own internal protection covers the receptacle — it does not substitute for the 625.54 GFCI, and it does nothing for the 625.56 enclosure duty.

sections.title: Article 626 — Electrified Truck Parking Spaces
sections.plain_explanation: Intro: shore-power connections at truck parking spaces — pedestals, receptacles, and disconnects that let a parked truck run its cab loads without idling. Commercial/industrial work; recognize the article when a truck-stop or warehouse job specs electrified spaces.
sections.on_the_job: Price electrified spaces from the pedestal schedule: count the spaces, confirm the receptacle type and the disconnect for each space, and treat each pedestal like a small service with its own grounding — not like a receptacle add on a site-lighting circuit.

sections.plain_explanation:

sections.title: Article 640 — Audio Signal Processing, Amplification, and Reproduction Equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 640 covers the power and wiring rules for audio signal processing, amplification and reproduction equipment — the professional and commercial sound systems in studios, performance venues, houses of worship and distributed-audio fit-outs.
• Line-voltage power to the equipment — the rack circuits — follows the general rules of Chapters 1 through 4 as Article 640 modifies them.
• The audio side — speaker wiring and signal cabling — follows Article 640's own wiring rules, and it is not interchangeable with line-voltage wiring.
• Most of the article lands on the specialty AV contractor. Sharma touches it when a commercial fit-out includes distributed audio and somebody has to feed the rack.
sections.on_the_job: A restaurant fit-out with distributed audio shows the split. Sharma's bid carries the rack power — two 20 A branch circuits to the AV rack location, the circuit size we install as a commercial minimum — and the AV contractor owns the speaker wiring, pulled and terminated under Article 640. Settle who owns what before rough-in: line-voltage power and low-voltage audio cable follow different rules and different trades' habits, and that split belongs in the bid, not in a change order at trim.
sections.why_it_exists: A sound system puts two very different kinds of wiring in the same rack and the same ceiling: 120 V power that can start a fire, and speaker cable carrying signals that pick up every bit of noise nearby. Run them like one system and you get hum in the speakers, line voltage where nobody expects it, and faults on cable that was never built for it. The article keeps the two sides separated and gives each its own rules.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating speaker cable like any other low-voltage wire that can ride along with power: 'it's only speaker wire — run it in the rack power conduit.' Article 640 gives the audio side its own wiring rules, and mixing the two sides in one raceway is exactly what the article is written to prevent. The scope trap runs the other way too: assuming the whole sound system is the AV contractor's problem when nobody has scoped the line-voltage rack power.

sections.title: Article 645 — Information Technology Equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Intro: special wiring allowances for IT equipment rooms that meet the article's conditions — including wiring under raised floors and the room disconnecting means. The allowances apply only when every condition in 645.4 is met; otherwise Chapters 1–4 govern as usual.

The room-level items Sharma would actually wire: a disconnecting means for the IT equipment — and for the dedicated HVAC serving the room — with remote disconnect controls at approved locations readily accessible in case of fire to authorized personnel and emergency responders (645.10(A)); the HVAC disconnect must also cause required fire/smoke dampers to close., and underfloor branch circuits run only in the wiring methods 645.5 permits. The disconnect button at the door is the visible part of this article on a data-room job, and its location is settled at rough-in, not at trim. 645.10 also allows the remote disconnect controls to cover designated zones within the room, and there is an exception for Critical Operations Data Systems.
sections.on_the_job: Before using any 645 allowance — underfloor wiring, the room disconnect arrangement — verify the room meets every condition in 645.4: dedicated IT room, the required disconnecting means, separation, and fire protection as the article lists them. If one condition fails, wire the room under Chapters 1 through 4 like any other space.

sections.title: Article 646 — Modular Data Centers
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 646 covers modular data centers: factory-built, prefabricated units rated 600 volts or less — an outer enclosure housing racks or cabinets of information technology equipment plus the support equipment, power distribution and cooling, that runs them. The article was added in the 2014 cycle; it is not new in 2020.
• A listed module is treated as listed equipment: it complies with the specific sections the article points to, and its internal wiring is the manufacturer's listing — the listing route commonly runs through UL's Subject 2755 outline for modular data centers. A module that is not listed must comply with Article 646 in full.
• 646.5: a nameplate on each enclosure gives the full-load current and the short-circuit current rating. Supply conductors are sized at not less than 125 percent of the nameplate full-load current.
• 646.9: flexible cords and cables listed for extra-hard usage may interconnect separate module enclosures — but may never connect a module to an external power source such as the building service.
• 646.18: space about electrical equipment inside the module complies with 110.26.
• 646.19: for equipment over 6 ft wide or deep, there is an entrance to and egress from the working space at each end, each at least 24 in. wide and 6½ ft high, with listed panic hardware or listed fire exit hardware. A single entrance is permitted only where 646.19(A) or (B) is met.
sections.on_the_job: Treat the module as listed equipment: Sharma's scope is the supply feeder, the disconnect, and the grounding connection landed on the module's marked terminals. Never field-modify the module's internal wiring to make a site condition fit — that is the manufacturer's listing you would be voiding. Worked example: a module lands on a pad behind a Winter Park warehouse with a nameplate full-load current of 160 A. The supply conductors are sized at 125 percent — 200 A minimum — before any other adjustment, and the feeder lands only on the marked supply terminals. The nameplate stays visible after the unit is set; if the pad layout parks it against a wall, that is a punch item, not a detail.

sections.why_it_exists: A modular data center packs a room's worth of energized distribution into a steel box with room for one person to work. If a fault or fire starts at the far end, the only safe direction is out — which is why the article fixes the working space and the exits at the factory instead of leaving them to whoever sets the box on the pad.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering 646.19 with 110.26(C)(2): that trigger is 1200 A. Article 646's trigger is size — equipment over 6 ft wide or deep needs an entrance at each end whatever its ampere rating.

sections.title: Article 647 — Sensitive Electronic Equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 647 covers a special power system for sensitive electronic equipment: a 120 V, single-phase system whose transformer secondary is center-tapped, with the center tap grounded, so each ungrounded leg sits at 60 V to ground while the voltage between the legs stays 120 V.
• The two legs are equal and opposite to ground — that balance is what cancels the ground noise that hums through audio and video work.
• The system has its own receptacle and grounding rules; receptacles are identified for this system so ordinary equipment is not plugged into it by mistake.
• It is rare, and it is always an engineered installation — nobody wires one from habit.
sections.on_the_job: If a studio or production client asks for 'clean power,' do not improvise a balanced 60/60 system in the field — it is an engineered installation with its own identified receptacles and grounding arrangement. Route the request to Mike for a design before anyone quotes it. And if you ever meter one that is already installed: each slot reads about 60 V to ground, and the two slots read 120 V to each other. On a normal circuit that reading means a lost neutral; on a 647 system it is exactly right.
sections.why_it_exists: Production audio and video gear picks up noise through its ground connections, and on a normal circuit that noise lands in the recording. With both legs balanced at 60 V to ground, noise coupled equally onto the two legs cancels instead of adding. The same balance is the hazard if it is improvised: a receptacle that looks normal but carries 60 V on both slots confuses the next person who meters it or plugs into it — which is why the system uses identified receptacles and an engineered design.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answers are 'a 60 V system' and 'wire it like a normal 120 V circuit.' It is a 120 V system — 120 V leg to leg — and neither leg is a grounded neutral you can treat like one. The field trap is worse: building a 'balanced' feed out of a standard transformer hookup because the client asked for clean power. Article 647 work is engineered, or it is not done.

sections.title: Article 650 — Pipe Organs
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 650 covers the electrical circuits and parts of electrically operated pipe organs that control the sounding apparatus and the keyboards — the action system. Electronic organs are a different animal: 650.3 sends them to Article 640.
• 650.4: the action runs on dc from a transformer-type rectifier, and the dc potential must not exceed 30 volts.
• 650.5: the rectifier is bonded to the equipment grounding conductor under Article 250 — the case is grounded, the low-voltage output is the working circuit.
• 650.6(A): conductor minimums are tiny and specific — 28 AWG for electronic signal circuits, 26 AWG for electromagnetic valve supply and the like, and the main common-return conductor in the electromagnetic supply not less than 14 AWG.
• 650.6(B)–(D): conductors carry thermoplastic or thermosetting insulation, are cabled together outside the organ proper, and each cable gets an outer covering — flame-spread resistant where the cable is not in metal raceway.
• 650.7: cables are fastened in place, may attach directly to the organ structure, and must not lie in contact with other conductors.
• 650.8: circuits are arranged so the 26 AWG and 28 AWG conductors are protected by an overcurrent device rated not more than 6 amperes.
sections.on_the_job: On a church job with an organ, coordinate two separate scopes: the blower is an ordinary motor circuit under Article 430, and the low-voltage action wiring is the organ builder's listed system. Sharma's rough-in is the line-voltage side — a 20 A branch circuit to the blower disconnect and a 20 A circuit feeding the rectifier location the builder picks. Get the builder's power requirements before rough-in — organs are usually discovered in the attic conversation, not on the electrical drawings.
sections.why_it_exists: An organ action system is hundreds of hair-thin conductors bundled through a wooden chamber full of dust, bellows, and century-old timber. A short on an unfused 28 AWG conductor cannot trip a normal breaker — it just glows. The 30-volt cap, the 6-ampere fuse cap, and the cabling rules keep a fault in that bundle from becoming a church fire.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the whole organ as one low-voltage system. The action circuits are capped at 30 volts dc by 650.4 — but the blower that feeds the wind is a line-voltage motor, wired and protected under Article 430 like any other motor.

Cotton- or enamel-insulated legacy wire reused instead of thermoplastic or thermosetting insulation (650.6(B)).
Rectifier case left unbonded from the equipment grounding conductor (650.5).

sections.title: Article 660 — X-Ray Equipment
sections.plain_explanation: Intro: disconnect, control, and transformer rules for medical, dental, and industrial X-ray equipment, including the momentary-rating allowances for diagnostic equipment. Healthcare work coordinates with Article 517.
sections.on_the_job: On a dental or medical fit-out, get the X-ray equipment's momentary and long-time ratings from the manufacturer before sizing its branch circuit — diagnostic equipment demand is figured on the momentary rating, and sizing from the tube's headline number alone undersizes the circuit. sections.title: Article 665 — Induction and Dielectric Heating Equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 665 covers the construction and installation of induction heating, induction melting, induction welding and dielectric heating equipment and accessories for industrial and scientific applications (665.1). Medical and dental applications, appliances, and line-frequency pipeline and vessel heating sit outside it — pipeline heating lives in Article 427.
• Wiring from the source of power to the equipment follows Chapters 1 through 4 unless this article amends it (665.3).
• The equipment stays out of hazardous (classified) locations unless it and its wiring are approved for that location (665.4).
• The output circuit — everything external to the converting device — may be isolated from ground, and its current to ground is limited so that no 50 V or more to ground appears on any accessible part (665.5).
• Multiple control points are interlocked so the applicator can be energized from only one point at a time, with a way to de-energize at every point; foot switches get a shield against accidental closing (665.7).
• Supply conductor ampacity is built from the nameplate ratings of the largest group of equipment that can operate at the same time, plus the standby currents of the remaining equipment (665.10).
sections.on_the_job: Industrial only for Sharma: if a bid shows induction or dielectric heating, price only the supply disconnect and feeder shown on the engineered drawings. The disconnect belongs within sight of the equipment and capable of being locked in the open position (665.12). The equipment's shielding, guarding and interlocks are the manufacturer's listing — not field work, and not value-engineering targets. If the drawings don't show the supply, that is an RFI, not an allowance.

sections.why_it_exists: This equipment makes heat with high-frequency energy, and the output side does not behave like a branch circuit: RF voltage can appear on frames and nearby metal, capacitors hold a charge after shutdown, and an applicator energized from a second control point can start while a worker's hands are in it. The interlock, guarding and bonding rules exist because the hazard is invisible energy, not a sparking fault you can see coming.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the output circuit like ordinary wiring that has to be grounded — 665.5 permits it isolated from ground, and grounding it 'to be safe' can defeat the design. The second trap is sizing the feeder by adding every nameplate on the floor: 665.10 counts the largest group that can run at once at full rating and the rest at standby current.
inspection_fails: Applicator can be energized from two control stations at once — control points not interlocked.
Foot switch with no shield over the contact button.
Feeder sized from Chapter 3 habits instead of the 665.10 nameplate method.
Equipment frames not bonded — RF voltage standing on exposed metal (665.26).

sections.title: Article 668 — Electrolytic Cells
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 668 covers electrolytic cells — the cell lines that make chlorine, caustic, aluminum and similar products by passing heavy DC current through a process. The recognition points:
• A cell line and its DC process power supply, inside the cell line working zone, are treated as one functional unit — a single line can run over 400,000 A DC at over 1000 V DC.
• Inside the zone, ordinary grounding logic is reversed on purpose. The DC process power supply conductors are not required to be grounded (668.11).
• Where that supply runs over 50 V between conductors, its metal enclosures are grounded through protective relaying or by a copper bonding conductor not smaller than 2/0 AWG (668.11).
• AC systems and exposed conductive surfaces inside the zone are not required to be grounded (668.30); the workers and their tools are insulated from ground instead.
• Any part of a crane or hoist that contacts an energized cell or its attachments must be insulated from ground (668.32).
• Each DC power supply to a cell line must be capable of being disconnected; a removable link in the busbar can be that disconnecting means (668.13).
• Outside the working zone, none of this applies — the rest of the NEC governs in full (668.3).
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only. If a scope ever shows a rectifier room, a cell line, or busbar runs feeding process tanks at a Florida chemical or plating plant, that is Article 668 territory — heavy industrial, and not Sharma work. Flag it to Sanjay and Mike the day it appears in a scope. If Sharma ever services ordinary building equipment in such a plant, that work sits outside the working zone and follows the normal rules — but nobody from a residential crew improvises inside the zone.
sections.why_it_exists: Cell line crews have to touch energized cell surfaces to run the process — the work cannot be done with everything dead and grounded. If the line, the tools and the crane were grounded the ordinary way, the worker would become the bridge between live parts and ground. So the article insulates the worker and the workplace from ground, and keeps the DC system floating, instead of insulating the conductor.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the ordinary-practice answer: ground the DC conductors, ground the crane, ground the tools, and apply 110.26 working-space logic inside the zone. Inside the cell line working zone that is exactly backwards — 668.11 does not require the process conductors to be grounded, 668.32 requires crane parts contacting cells to be insulated from ground, and 668.3 keeps the ordinary articles for work outside the zone.
inspection_fails: Cell line treated as an ordinary grounded system — process conductors grounded against the 668.11 design.
Crane hook block contacting energized cells with no insulation from ground (668.32).
Portable tools in the zone fed from an ordinary grounded receptacle circuit instead of an isolated, ungrounded supply (668.20).
DC power supply with no means of being disconnected from its cell line (668.13).

sections.title: Article 669 — Electroplating
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 669 covers the electrical components and accessory equipment that supply power and controls for electroplating — and anodizing, electropolishing and electrostripping ride under the same rules; the Code calls all of it electroplating (669.1). This is industrial work: a rectifier feeds plating tanks at low voltage and very high current, often over bare busbar instead of ordinary branch-circuit wiring.
• Equipment must be identified for electroplating service (669.3).
• Branch-circuit conductors supplying the equipment need an ampacity of at least 125% of the total connected load (669.5).
• Busbars follow 366.23: bare copper busbar is capped at 1000 A per square inch of cross-section (669.5).
• At 60 V DC or less, insulated conductors may run without insulated supports if protected from physical damage, and bare copper or aluminum may run supported on insulators (669.6(A)).
• Over 60 V DC, insulated conductors need insulated supports, and bare conductors on insulators must be guarded against accidental contact up to the point of termination (669.6(B)).
• More than one power supply means a disconnecting means on the DC side of each supply (669.8(A)).
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only for Sharma. On an industrial bid for a plating shop, the rectifier nameplate and the plant engineer's busbar design drive everything. Say the connected load is 400 A of DC plating load: the branch circuit is sized at 500 A minimum (125%), and the bare copper busbar needs at least half a square inch of cross-section at the 1000 A per square inch cap — before voltage drop even enters the talk. Do not price plating-line conductors from Chapter 3 ampacity habits: the job needs the plant engineer's design before it needs an electrician.

sections.why_it_exists: A plating line is a burn and fire hazard wearing a low-voltage disguise. The volts sound harmless, but hundreds of amps through one loose busbar joint makes heat fast, and a DC arc does not self-extinguish at a zero crossing the way AC does. The 125% conductor rule, the busbar density cap and the guarding rules above 60 V exist because the failure mode is a glowing joint or an accidental touch in a wet, conductive chemical shop — not a tripped breaker.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the supply like an ordinary Chapter 3 branch circuit — conductor ampacity equal to the load, or busbar picked by eye. 669.5 demands 125% of the total connected load, and busbar is capped by current density under 366.23, not by a Table 310.16 lookup. The other wrong answer is 'it is only 48 volts, so it is harmless' — at plating currents, low voltage is exactly where the burn hazard lives.
inspection_fails: Busbar joint discolored and hot — the run was pushed past the 1000 A per square inch density cap.
Branch circuit sized at 100% of the rectifier load — the 125% factor of 669.5 never applied.
Bare busbar over 60 V DC run where a worker can brush against it — no guarding to the termination.
Two rectifiers feeding one line, one disconnect — no DC-side disconnect for the second supply.

sections.title: Article 670 — Industrial Machinery
sections.plain_explanation:
Intro: the nameplate, supply-conductor, and overcurrent rules for industrial machines with combined motor and control loads. The machine's nameplate (670.3(A)) supplies the full-load current, SCCR and largest-motor data, and 670.4(A) sets the supply-conductor ampacity: not less than 125% of the full-load current of all resistance heating loads, plus 125% of the full-load current of the highest-rated motor, plus the full-load currents of all other connected motors and apparatus that may run at the same time (based on duty cycle). Use the supply-conductor ampacity the machine's nameplate/documentation states per 670.4(A) — not a 430 calculation.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 670.1: Revised Section 670.1 to now include overvoltage protection for supply conductors for industrial machinery.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a machine whose nameplate gives a supply-circuit rating of 46 A is fed with conductors of at least that ampacity — use the supply-conductor ampacity the machine's nameplate/documentation states per 670.4(A) — not by opening the machine and adding its internal motors under 430. Photograph the nameplate for the takeoff; it is the calculation.

sections.title: Article 675 — Electrically Driven or Controlled Irrigation Machines
sections.plain_explanation: Intro: center-pivot and similar irrigation machines — collector rings, grounding, and the disconnect that must be able to stop the whole machine. Agricultural work across Sharma's rural counties.
sections.on_the_job: On a center-pivot call, open and lock the machine disconnect before touching collector rings or span wiring — a pivot can be started remotely by the farm's controls. Then check the grounding and bonding at the pivot point; lightning damage and a cut ground are the usual Florida service finds.

sections.title: Article 680 — Swimming Pools, Fountains, and Similar Installations
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 680 is organized by installation type, and the first job on any pool is knowing which part you are in: Part I general rules ride with every part; Part II is permanently installed pools; Part III storable pools; Part IV spas and hot tubs; Part V fountains; Part VII hydromassage bathtubs; Part VIII pool lifts. Two systems run through all of it and must never be confused: grounding (the fault path back to the source) and equipotential bonding under 680.26 (tying everything a swimmer can touch to one potential). Florida is pool country — this is the highest-value article in the chapter for Sharma.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 680.10: Pool heat pumps and chillers finally have their own rule: listed, and wired by the nameplate. The 48-amp element split and 125 percent sizing now belong to resistance heaters only. Electric heat pumps and chillers that heat or cool pool water must be listed and installed to their nameplate ratings (680.10(B)).
• 680.14: Wiring in corrosive pool areas now has to be suitable for the location. LFNC joins the accepted list, aluminum conduit and tubing are out, and other equipment gets its own rule. Aluminum conduit and aluminum tubing aren't allowed in a corrosive pool environment (680.14(A)).
• 680.5: Pool ground-fault protection now depends on voltage to ground: Class A GFCI up to 150 volts to ground, and special purpose GFCI (SPGFCI) above 150 volts, up to 480 volts phase to phase. On circuits above 150 volts to ground, through 480 volts phase to phase, the device must be a special purpose GFCI (SPGFCI), 20 mA max.
• 680.54: New 680.54(C) brings pool-style equipotential bonding to splash pads and settles where to measure from: the walking area and collection basin are the shell, and their outer edge is the inside wall. Splash pads now need equipotential bonding the way pools do, including the bonded perimeter surface around them (680.54(C)).
• Article 680: Article 680 underwent a major reorganization to improve usability and compliance with the NEC Style Manual.
• 680.12: Text at Section 680.12 has been revised and subdivided to require equipment rooms, vaults, or pits with equipment to have drainage or be suitable for submersion in first-level subdivision A. New first-level subdivision B requires a 125-volt, 15-or 20-ampere receptacle and requires any receptacle in the space rated 150 volts or less to be ground-fault circuit- interrupter (GFCI) protected.
• 680.32: Received substantiation to revise the tide and text of Section 680.32 to indicate that both ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) and special-purpose ground-fault circuit interrupter (SPGFCI) requirements are covered in this section and add a reference back to 680.S(B) and (C).
• 680.44: Revised Section 680.44 to indicate that both GFCI and SPGFCI requirements are addressed for spa and hot tub installations.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Overhead conductor clearances
sections.plain_explanation:
In the 2020 edition the overhead rules live at 680.9(A) with Table 680.9(A) — older sources that cite 680.8 are working from a previous edition. The clearance in any direction from the water level, the edge of a diving structure, or the base of a diving platform is 22.5 ft for the conductors the table covers. Measured from maximum water level, the clearance to an observation stand, tower, or diving platform is 14.5 ft. All clearances are measured from maximum water level, not from the deck. Read Table 680.9(A) by its rows: the figures apply to the conductor types and voltages the table lists, measured as the table directs — they are not a blanket clearance for every wire over water. Overhead communications conductors and cables have their own rule at 680.9(B): a horizontal clearance of at least 10 ft from the pool and its associated structures.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 680.9(A): In Section 680.9(A), clarifies that open overhead wiring in raceways is not subject to the clearance requirements in Table 680.9(A) and Figure 680.9(A).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Underground wiring
sections.plain_explanation:
Underground wiring is not permitted under a pool, or within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall of the pool, unless it is necessary to supply pool equipment permitted by this article. That one sentence decides most pool-deck trenching before it starts.
• Wiring that does run in the 5 ft zone uses the article's methods: rigid metal conduit, intermediate metal conduit, rigid polyvinyl chloride conduit, reinforced thermosetting resin conduit, or Type MC cable, suitable for the conditions at that location.
• Minimum cover for those runs comes from Table 300.5 — in general locations, 6 in. for rigid and intermediate metal conduit and 18 in. for rigid PVC and RTRC.
• Equipment grounding for anything in the zone follows the pool rules of this article, not the general rules alone.
• When in doubt, route around the 5 ft band. A longer trench outside the band is almost always cheaper than a failed inspection inside it.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Park pool job, the equipment pad sits 4 ft from the water's edge, so the pump and heater feeds cross the band: they run in rigid PVC at 18 in. of cover, the minimum Table 300.5 asks of PVC in a general location. The site-lighting conduit for the back fence tells the other half of the story — it does not serve the pool, so it stays outside the 5 ft band even though cutting the corner would save 30 ft of trench. Keep site lighting and landscape conduits out of the band unless they serve the pool itself.

nec2023_change.change: Underground runs within 5 ft of a pool's inside wall now count as suitable only when the wiring method is installed as a complete system, from one outlet, junction or splice point to the next. The underground methods for the zone within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall now count only when installed as complete systems (680.11(A)).

sections.why_it_exists: Water, bare feet, and a faulted buried conductor are a bad mix: a damaged cable under a deck can put voltage into the water and the wet concrete around it, and a swimmer has no way to let go or step away. Keeping foreign wiring out of the band — and the wiring that must cross it inside a tough raceway, buried deep — keeps pool faults on pool equipment, where the bonding and GFCI rules can manage them.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is "any conduit, buried deep, is fine in the band." Depth is only half the rule — the method list in 680.11 is closed, and under the pool itself the answer is simpler: nothing runs there except what the pool equipment needs.
inspection_fails: Direct-buried UF cable crossing the 5 ft band to feed landscape lighting.
Conduit run under the pool shell as a shortcut to the equipment pad.
Rigid PVC in the band buried with only a few inches of cover instead of the Table 300.5 minimum.
Site-lighting or irrigation wiring threaded through the band when a route outside it existed.

sections.title: Motor wiring and equipment grounding conductor
sections.plain_explanation:
Pool motor circuits carry an equipment grounding conductor with two pool differences from ordinary motor work:
• The EGC is insulated copper — not a bare conductor in the raceway, and not aluminum.
• It is sized from Table 250.122 by the overcurrent device ahead of the circuit — but never smaller than 12 AWG, even where the table would allow smaller.
The one place the floor bites: a 15 A circuit, where Table 250.122 pairs the breaker with a 14 AWG copper EGC. On a pool motor circuit that 14 AWG stays in the truck — the EGC is 12 AWG. At 20 A the table and the floor agree on 12 AWG; at 30 A and above the table takes over (10 AWG at 30, 40 and 60 A).
sections.on_the_job: Florida pool pad, new build: the pump motor is fed from a 20 A GFCI breaker (680.21(C)) in the Siemens panel. The crew pulls two circuit conductors and a green insulated 12 AWG copper EGC in the raceway to the motor — the table size for 20 A and the 680.21(A) floor are the same number here. On the same pad, a 15 A circuit for a small auxiliary pump still gets a 12 AWG insulated EGC, not the 14 AWG the table alone would allow.
sections.figure_idea: Equipment pad raceway opened: insulated green EGC alongside the circuit conductors.
sections.why_it_exists: The equipment pad is wet, outdoors, and tied into the pool's equipotential bonding. A bare ground wire in a damp raceway corrodes quietly for years, and the first anyone knows is when a fault has no path back and the breaker never trips — with swimmers in the water. The insulated copper conductor, held to a 12 AWG floor, keeps the fault path intact so the overcurrent device opens fast.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the pool EGC straight off Table 250.122 and stopping there: 14 AWG for a 15 A circuit is the table's answer for ordinary work, and it is the wrong answer at a pool. 680.21(A) sets a floor of 12 AWG and requires the conductor to be insulated copper — a bare ground pulled in the conduit fails even at the right size.
inspection_fails: Bare equipment grounding conductor in the pool motor raceway — 680.21(A) requires it insulated.
14 AWG EGC on a 15 A pool motor circuit — below the 12 AWG floor.
Aluminum EGC on a pool motor circuit — the section requires copper.
EGC sized by the conductor size instead of by the overcurrent device ahead of it (Table 250.122).

sections.title: GFCI protection for pool motors — re-checked
sections.plain_explanation:
GFCI protection is required for outlets supplying pool motors on branch circuits rated 150V or less to ground and 60A or less, single-phase or three-phase — by receptacle or by direct connection. This was one of the figures re-checked against 2020-based sources before this chapter was written, and the v1 lookup (L-088) states it correctly: the scope is all pool motors inside those ratings, not just cord-and-plug pumps.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 680.21: Repairing a pool pump motor now triggers ground-fault protection, just like replacing one. The device matches the circuit: a GFCI, or a special purpose GFCI (SPGFCI) above 150 volts to ground. Repair now counts: a pump motor covered by 680.21(C) that's repaired, not only one that's replaced, needs ground-fault protection on its circuit (680.21(D)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: A hardwired 240V pool pump needs GFCI protection just as much as a plug-in one — plan the protection device at design, not at the final walk.

sections.title: Replacement pump motors
sections.plain_explanation:
680.21(D) is a service rule: where a pool pump motor is replaced, the replacement work must provide the GFCI protection 680.21(C) requires for that outlet. A service call that swaps a motor on an old unprotected circuit does not get to leave it unprotected.
• The duty rides with the replacement, not with the age of the pool — an existing unprotected circuit is not grandfathered once the motor is changed.
• The (C) scope it points back to: outlets supplying pool motors on branch circuits rated 150 V or less to ground and 60 A or less, single-phase or three-phase, by receptacle or by direct connection.
sections.on_the_job: Service crews: a motor swap triggers the GFCI upgrade — quote it with the replacement, not as a surprise. A typical Florida call is a 240 V, 20 A hard-wired pump on a plain breaker: the replacement price carries the GFCI protection up front, and the tech verifies protection at the outlet before the new motor is left running — not after the callback.

nec2023_change.change: The revisions at 680.21(D) expand the requirement to provide ground- fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) protection for replaced pool pump motors and also include those that are repaired, but not replaced.

sections.title: Receptacles — the 2020 lettering
sections.plain_explanation: The 2020 lettering, re-checked before writing: (A)(1) the required receptacle for a permanently installed pool — not less than 6 ft and not more than 20 ft from the inside wall of the pool, and not more than 6 ft 6 in. above the floor, platform, or grade serving the pool. (A)(2) receptacles serving pool circulation and sanitation equipment — not less than 6 ft away, grounding type, GFCI protected. (A)(3) all other receptacles — not less than 6 ft from the inside wall. (A)(4) GFCI protection for all 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles located within 20 ft of the inside wall. (A)(5) a pool equipment room needs at least one 125V 15A or 20A receptacle and GFCI protection for receptacles in the room. (A)(6) distances are measured as the shortest path a supply cord would follow without passing through a floor, wall, ceiling, doorway, window, or other effective barrier. Older sources print different letters for the same rules — cite the 2020 letters.
sections.on_the_job: Lay out the required receptacle in the 6–20 ft band at rough-in, and remember the tape follows the cord path, not a straight line through a screen wall.
sections.figure_idea: Plan view: 6 ft inner line, 20 ft outer line, required receptacle between them; cord-path measurement around a barrier.
sections.florida_note: Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020.

sections.title: Lighting and fans over and near the pool
sections.plain_explanation: New luminaires, lighting outlets, and ceiling fans installed above a pool or within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall must be at least 12 ft above maximum water level (B)(1). Existing luminaires and fans in that zone may remain where they are at least 5 ft above the water, rigidly attached, and GFCI protected (B)(3). In the band from 5 to 10 ft horizontally, luminaires need GFCI protection unless they are at least 5 ft above the water and rigidly attached (B)(4). Listed low-voltage luminaires have their own path through 680.23(A)(2) (B)(6).
sections.on_the_job: Screen-enclosure and lanai lights over Florida pools land in this section constantly — measure from maximum water level, not the deck.
sections.figure_idea: Elevation: new fixture at 12 ft over water; existing fixture grandfathered at 5 ft with GFCI.

sections.title: Switching devices — 5 ft from the water
sections.plain_explanation: Switching devices — the switches that control pool-area equipment and lighting — are located at least 5 ft horizontally from the inside wall of the pool, spa, or hot tub, unless they are separated from the water by a permanent barrier such as a solid wall or fence that keeps a person in the water from reaching the switch. The measurement follows the same thinking as the receptacle rules in 680.22(A): distance is about what a wet hand can reach, not about where the device looks convenient on the plan. Switches that are part of a listed assembly, or that the article specifically permits closer in, are exceptions to read on the equipment itself — not a general permission.
sections.on_the_job: Put the pool light switch and the pump control on the house wall or the equipment pad, outside the 5 ft line, at rough-in. The classic correction is a switch roughed in on the pool-side face of a screen enclosure post, within reach of the water.
sections.figure_idea: Plan view: 5 ft switching-device line around the water, barrier exception shown at a fence.

sections.title: Underwater luminaires
sections.plain_explanation:
Underwater luminaires must be listed for the purpose and installed by niche type — wet-niche, dry-niche, or no-niche — with transformers and power supplies for low-voltage units listed for pool use under 680.23(A)(2). Units operating above the low-voltage contact limit get GFCI protection. Wall-mounted units sit with the top of the lens at least 18 in. below the normal water level unless the luminaire is listed and marked for use at a lesser depth.

The 'low-voltage contact limit' this section leans on is a defined term (680.2): not more than 15 V AC sinusoidal (RMS), 21.2 V peak for nonsinusoidal AC, or 30 V for continuous DC, with its own limits for interrupted DC. A listed low-voltage luminaire system at or under that limit is the path that avoids GFCI protection for the luminaire circuit; anything operating above the limit is GFCI protected. When a pool-light quote says 'low voltage,' confirm which side of that definition the system sits on before the protection is priced.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 680.23(B)(2)(a): Substantiation was received that rigid metal conduit extending directly to wet niche luminaires in forming shells of pools must be as listed red brass or listed stainless steel.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: The light, its niche, its transformer, and its junction box are one system — check all four against the listing.
sections.figure_idea: Wet-niche luminaire cross-section with the 18 in. lens depth marked.

sections.title: Junction boxes for underwater luminaires
sections.plain_explanation: A junction box tied to a conduit running directly to an underwater luminaire forming shell must be listed, labeled, and identified as a swimming pool junction box, located not less than 4 ft from the inside wall of the pool (unless separated by a solid fence, wall, or other permanent barrier), and at an elevation of not less than 4 in. above the ground or pool deck, or not less than 8 in. above maximum water level — whichever gives the greater elevation. A flush deck box is permitted only for systems at or below the low-voltage contact limit, and still at least 4 ft out.
sections.on_the_job: Set the deck box on the tape and the level at rough-in; 'close enough' fails on both numbers.
sections.figure_idea: Deck box elevation sketch — 8 in. above max water, 4 in. above deck, 4 ft from inside wall.

sections.title: Feeders supplying pool equipment panelboards
sections.plain_explanation: Where a feeder supplies a panelboard that serves pool, spa, or fountain equipment, 680.25 holds the feeder to a stricter standard than an ordinary feeder. The feeder is installed in one of the wiring methods the section lists — rigid or intermediate metal conduit, rigid PVC conduit, or another identified raceway — and it must carry an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor, sized from Table 250.122 but never smaller than 12 AWG. The point of the insulated grounding conductor is the same as in 680.21(A) for motors: around water, the fault path is a real insulated wire, not the raceway alone and not a bare conductor in the dirt.
sections.on_the_job: Feeding a pool subpanel from the house panel: pull an insulated copper ground with the feeder, 12 AWG minimum even on a small feeder, and keep the run in raceway. A feeder roughed in cable with a bare ground is the correction waiting to happen.
sections.figure_idea: Feeder run from house panel to pool panelboard: raceway shown, insulated EGC called out at 12 AWG minimum.
sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): The wiring-method list looks incomplete: the page names only RMC, IMC, PVC or 'another identified raceway', but the code list also includes LFMC, LFNC, RTRC, EMT (on or within a building), ENT (within a building) and Type MC (within a building, not in a corrosive environment), plus an exception for existing feeders. I also could not confirm first-hand whether NEC 2020 still requires the feeder EGC to be INSULATED in 680.25(B) — the 2020 cycle changed several Article 680 grounding/wiring-method rules. Check 680.25(A) and (B) against the printed 2020 text, then publish the full list and the confirmed EGC wording. 'Table 250.122, not smaller than 12 AWG' is consistent with earlier editions.

sections.title: Equipotential bonding — the idea
sections.plain_explanation: Bonding around a pool is not grounding. Its job is to tie everything a swimmer can touch into one equipotential mass so there is no voltage difference between the water, the deck, a ladder, and the pump — because it is the difference, not the voltage alone, that drives current through a person. The bonding system is not required to extend back to a panelboard, a service disconnect, or a grounding electrode, and it never substitutes for the equipment grounding conductor in the branch circuit.
sections.on_the_job: Two systems, two purposes: the green EGC carries fault current home; the bare 8 AWG bonding grid kills voltage differences. Crews who can say that sentence pass pool inspections.
sections.figure_idea: Swimmer touching a ladder and the water, both bonded to the same grid — no potential difference arrows.

sections.title: Equipotential bonding — what gets bonded, and how
sections.plain_explanation: The parts in 680.26(B)(1) through (B)(7) are bonded together with a solid copper conductor not smaller than 8 AWG, connected with a listed pressure connector, a terminal bar, or another listed means per 250.8(A): (B)(1) conductive pool shells — the structural reinforcing steel, or the copper conductor grid that serves as the alternate where a conductive shell's steel is encapsulated in a nonconductive compound or is not available. A nonconductive shell (vinyl, fiberglass) is not a conductive shell at all and needs no shell bonding grid; (B)(2) perimeter surfaces (next page); (B)(3) metallic components; (B)(4) underwater lighting forming shells and mounting brackets; (B)(5) metal fittings larger than 4 in. that penetrate the shell; (B)(6) electrical equipment — with the (B)(6)(a) rule for double-insulated pump motors: the double-insulated motor itself is NOT bonded; instead an 8 AWG solid copper bonding conductor is provided at the grid so a future replacement motor that is not double-insulated can be bonded; and (B)(7) fixed metal parts within 5 ft horizontally of the inside walls (with the vertical-separation exception at 12 ft).
sections.on_the_job: Walk the (B) list physically at rough-in — shell, steel, fittings, equipment, nearby metal — before anything is buried or shot.
sections.figure_idea: Bonding grid plan with the seven (B) categories called out.

sections.title: Perimeter surfaces — the ring
sections.plain_explanation:
The bonded perimeter surface extends 3 ft beyond the inside walls of the pool. Where the ring method is used, it is one or more bare solid copper conductors not smaller than 8 AWG, laid 18 to 24 in. out from the inside walls and 4 to 6 in. below the subgrade, and attached to the pool's reinforcing steel or copper grid at a minimum of four uniformly spaced points. The perimeter rule exists so the deck a wet swimmer stands on is at the same potential as the water.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 680.26: Perimeter bonding depth is now measured from finished grade: no deeper than 6 in under paving, 4 to 6 in under bare ground. An interim amendment later rewrote the perimeter rules again. As printed in 2023, a copper ring or grid goes in or under paving, no more than 6 in below finished grade (680.26(B)(2)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Set the ring before pavers or deck pour — depth and distance are both inspection points, and neither can be fixed after the deck is down.
sections.figure_idea: Section through the deck edge: ring at 18–24 in. out, 4–6 in. below subgrade, tie points marked.
