sections.title: Pool water bonding — 9 square inches
sections.plain_explanation: The pool water itself must be bonded. Where a bonded part (a ladder rail, a light niche, a fitting) is already in direct contact with the water, that contact does the job. Where nothing bonded touches the water, an approved corrosion-resistant conductive surface of at least 9 sq in. must be in contact with it — the familiar listed water-bonding fitting in the skimmer or pump line.
sections.on_the_job: All-plastic pools with vinyl liners and no metal in the water are the trap — check for the 9 sq in. contact on every job.
sections.figure_idea: Skimmer with a listed water-bond plate, 9 sq in. dimensioned.

sections.title: Storable pools — Parts I and III only
sections.plain_explanation: A storable pool (and a storable spa or hot tub) is governed by Parts I and III of Article 680 — and 680.26 equipotential bonding does not apply to it. The pump and equipment rules of Part III substitute for the Part II regime. Classification is the whole game: the same backyard water is a different code job depending on whether the pool is storable or permanently installed. 'Storable' is a defined term, not a synonym for above-ground: under 680.2 a storable pool is one built to be stored away, with a maximum water depth of 42 in. and walls of nonmetallic molded polymeric construction or inflatable fabric. A permanently installed above-ground pool does not meet that definition and is Part II work, bonding included.
sections.on_the_job: Don't bond a storable pool like a gunite pool, and don't wire a permanent pool like a storable one — confirm which it is before the quote.

sections.title: Spas and hot tubs — Parts I and IV (outdoor adds Part II)
sections.plain_explanation: Spas and hot tubs are governed by Parts I and IV, and an outdoor spa also picks up the Part II rules that Part IV references (680.42) — receptacle distances, GFCI, and bonding arrive through that door. A self-contained factory spa package still lands on an installation that must meet the article; the listing doesn't waive the field wiring rules.
sections.on_the_job: Outdoor spa on a lanai: run the Part II checklist (distances, GFCI, bonding) even though the tub arrived as one box.

sections.title: Spa emergency shutoff — 5 ft, in sight, labeled
sections.plain_explanation:
Spas and hot tubs (other than at one-family dwellings) must have an emergency shutoff for the recirculation and jet system: readily accessible, adjacent to and within sight of the tub, at least 5 ft away from it, and clearly labeled as the emergency shutoff. The 5 ft floor keeps a person in the water from reaching it; the in-sight rule lets a bystander find it.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 680.41: Spas and hot tubs get an equipment setback in new 680.41(B): gear above the low-voltage contact limit needs 5 ft of horizontal distance from the inside wall unless a permanent barrier stands between. Anything above the low-voltage contact limit stays 5 ft or more, measured horizontally, from the inside wall of the spa or hot tub (680.41(B)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Hotels, condos, and amenity centers need the shutoff; a single-family backyard spa does not — know which job you're on before omitting it.
sections.figure_idea: Amenity-center spa with the labeled shutoff on the wall 5 ft away, in sight.

nec2023_change.change: Spas and hot tubs get an equipment setback in new 680.41(B): gear above the low-voltage contact limit needs 5 ft of horizontal distance from the inside wall unless a permanent barrier stands between. Anything above the low-voltage contact limit stays 5 ft or more, measured horizontally, from the inside wall of the spa or hot tub (680.41(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 680.41 Spa equipment setback

sections.title: Outdoor spas and hot tubs — Part II rides along (680.42)
sections.plain_explanation:
An outdoor spa or hot tub is not Part IV alone: 680.42 sends the installation back through Parts I and II as well. The Part II items that arrive with it are the ones crews most often miss on a packaged backyard unit:
• Receptacle distances and GFCI protection per 680.22(A) — the receptacle layout and protection are figured the same way as at a pool
• Equipotential bonding per 680.26 for the tub's equipment and the metal within reach of it — a factory-built tub does not waive the bonding
• The Part I disconnecting means (680.12): readily accessible, within sight of the equipment it serves, and at least 5 ft from the inside walls unless separated by a permanent barrier
A listed self-contained unit still lands on a field installation. Its listing covers the tub; the pad wiring, the bonding, the disconnect, and the receptacles around it are installed work under this article.
sections.on_the_job: Price an outdoor spa like a small pool: circuit, GFCI protection, bonding, disconnect, and receptacle layout all go on the takeoff as their own line items. The tub arriving in one crate changes none of them.
sections.figure_idea: Lanai spa with callouts: disconnect 5 ft away in sight of the tub, receptacle placed per 680.22(A), bonding conductor tying the tub equipment into the grid.
sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): Two likely errors, not confirmed first-hand. (1) "a factory-built tub does not waive the bonding" overstates it. Since 2017, 680.42 has relieved perimeter-surface equipotential bonding (680.26(B)(2)) for listed self-contained spas/hot tubs installed above a finished surface, under stated conditions, while the tub's own equipment bonding still applies. (2) In NEC 2020 the maintenance disconnecting means appears to be 680.13, not 680.12 (2020 added 680.14 Corrosive Environment and renumbered). Check both against the printed 2020 text, then correct the bullet and the citation.

sections.title: Indoor spas and hot tubs
sections.plain_explanation: An indoor spa or hot tub is wired under Parts I and II of Article 680 as modified by 680.43, and any Chapter 3 wiring method may be used. Receptacles [680.43(A)]: at least one 125V, 15A or 20A receptacle on a general-purpose branch circuit must be located not less than 6 ft and not more than 10 ft from the inside wall; every receptacle must be at least 6 ft from the inside walls, measured horizontally; 125-volt receptacles rated 30A or less within 10 ft of the inside walls must be GFCI protected; and a receptacle that supplies spa or hot tub equipment must be GFCI protected. Luminaires and ceiling fans within 5 ft horizontally of an inside wall must be at least 12 ft above the spa or hot tub or be GFCI protected [680.43(B)]. Switches must be at least 5 ft from the inside walls, measured horizontally [680.43(C)] — indoors, no permanent-barrier exception applies to that switch distance; the barrier language in this section belongs to bonding [680.43(D)], which ties together metal parts within 5 ft of the inside walls that are not separated from the spa or hot tub by a permanent barrier. The distances in this section are measured by the shortest path a cord would follow without piercing a floor, wall, ceiling, or other permanent barrier.
sections.on_the_job: Measure the 6 ft receptacle band and the 5 ft switch distance by the cord path around partitions, not a straight line through them — and do not let a partition talk you into a switch inside 5 ft; indoors, the barrier counts for bonding, not for switches.

sections.title: Spas and hot tubs — GFCI protection (680.44)
sections.plain_explanation: 680.44 is the protection rule for spas and hot tubs: the outlet supplying a spa or hot tub must have GFCI protection. Read it with the pages around it — the outdoor installations of 680.42 and the indoor installations of 680.43 — because the protection point, the wiring method and the bonding all have to land together on the same tub. Edition note: this page states the NEC 2020 rule Florida enforces; any 2023 change is confirmed against the printed 2023 text before it is taught here.
sections.on_the_job: On a spa or hot tub hookup, confirm the GFCI protection point before the tub is filled — breaker, receptacle or disconnect device — and test it at final with the tub's own equipment running.
sections.unverified_reason: New short page written 2026-11-25 per Mike Holt ruling 8 (the C6 checklists already cite 680.44). Verified=false until checked against the printed NEC 2020.

sections.title: Fountains — Parts I and V
sections.plain_explanation:
Fountains are governed by Part I (general) and Part V of Article 680. The parts are the first decision on the job:
• Decorative fountain nobody enters: Parts I and V.
• Interactive fountain, splash feature, or any fountain people can enter: the Part II rules the section references come in as well — treat the water like a pool.
• The equipment is pool-grade listed equipment: submersible pumps, luminaires, and their supplies. Landscape-lighting stock is not fountain equipment.
• Submersible equipment runs on GFCI protection (680.51(A)) — if it lives under fountain water on line voltage, it is GFCI protected.
sections.on_the_job: An HOA entry fountain in Florida is drawn as a dry-deck ornament, but the site plan shows steps into the basin and the sales brochure calls it a splash feature. That answer changes the wiring: the crew prices it as an enterable fountain, with the referenced Part II rules on top of Parts I and V, a listed submersible pump on GFCI protection, and listed fountain luminaires — not the landscape-lighting package the GC first suggested. Ask about entry before pricing, every time.

nec2023_change.change: Fountains now get the same 5 ft equipment rule as pools: anything above the low-voltage contact limit stays 5 ft from the inside wall unless a permanent barrier separates it. Gear running above the low-voltage contact limit needs at least 5 ft of separation from the fountain's inside wall (680.50(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 680.50 Fountain equipment setback

sections.why_it_exists: Water, electricity and bare feet are the pool problem in a smaller basin. A fountain looks harmless because it is shallow and decorative, but a fault in a submersible pump or luminaire puts voltage in water people touch — and on an interactive feature, children stand in it. Pool-grade listed equipment and GFCI protection are what keep a fault from becoming a shock.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that fountains live in Part II with the pools, or that a fountain is just landscape lighting that gets wet. 680.50 puts fountains in Parts I and V; Part II enters only through the reference, when people can get in the water. And the equipment is listed pool-grade equipment — a landscape transformer and a garden luminaire are not a fountain system.
inspection_fails: Landscape-lighting equipment installed as fountain luminaires — not listed fountain equipment.
Submersible pump with no GFCI protection (680.51(A)).
Interactive fountain wired as a dry-deck ornament — the referenced Part II rules were never applied.
Line-voltage equipment in the water that is not listed for fountain use.

sections.title: Fountains — GFCI for submersible equipment
sections.plain_explanation: Under 680.51(A), GFCI protection is required for fountain luminaires, submersible pumps, and other submersible equipment, unless the equipment is a listed low-voltage system supplied through the 680.23(A)(2) path. If it lives under fountain water and runs on line voltage, it is GFCI protected — no exceptions by habit.
sections.on_the_job: At rough-in, land every line-voltage fountain pump and luminaire on its GFCI device, and test the protection at startup with water in the basin. A fountain circuit that trips only when wet is a find-it-now problem — do not leave it as a callback or, worse, defeat the device to keep the water feature running.

sections.title: Hydromassage bathtubs — Part VII only
sections.plain_explanation: A hydromassage bathtub (the jetted tub in a bathroom) is governed by Part VII alone — it does not pick up the pool and spa parts. The unit must be on an individual branch circuit with readily accessible GFCI protection; 125V receptacles rated 30A or less within 6 ft of the tub need GFCI protection; the other electrical equipment in the room stays under Chapters 1–4 (680.72); and the equipment must remain accessible without damaging the building finish (680.73) — the access panel is a code item, not a courtesy.
sections.on_the_job: Master-bath remodels: dedicated circuit, accessible GFCI (a faceless device or GFCI breaker where the tub blocks access), and an access panel that actually opens.

sections.title: Pool lifts — Part VIII
sections.plain_explanation:
Part VIII of Article 680 covers electrically operated pool lifts — the accessibility lifts at commercial and amenity pools (the lift is defined in 680.2). Only Part I and Part VIII apply to the lift itself; the rest of Article 680 does not ride along.
• The lift must be listed, labeled and identified for swimming pool and spa use.
• A lift connected to premises wiring and operating above the low-voltage contact limit gets GFCI protection for personnel.
• The lift is bonded into the pool's equipotential bonding system — metal fittings attached to the pool structure under 680.26(B)(5) and fixed metal parts under 680.26(B)(7), with solid copper not smaller than 8 AWG.
• The listing exceptions are narrow: lifts running on a removable battery that is charged away from the pool, and small solar lifts, sit outside the listing rule. Read the exception before assuming one covers your lift.
sections.on_the_job: Amenity-pool ADA work at a Florida apartment community: the lift is electrical scope — include its circuit and bonding in the pool price, not as an afterthought allowance. On the rough-in that means a GFCI-protected circuit to the lift location and an 8 AWG solid copper bonding jumper tying the lift into the equipotential grid with the ladders and handrails. If the specified lift is a removable-battery model charged in the pump room, confirm the exception actually fits before deleting the circuit from the bid.

sections.why_it_exists: The lift carries a person with limited mobility into the water on a metal machine connected to premises power. If a fault energizes the frame, that user cannot jump clear. Listing proves the machine was built for wet service, GFCI protection cuts a ground fault in milliseconds, and bonding holds the lift, the water and the deck at one potential so no voltage difference can drive current through the swimmer.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the lift like pool furniture the GC sets in place — 'not electrical.' Part VIII makes it listed electrical equipment with GFCI and bonding duties. The reverse trap is bonding the lift back to the panelboard: equipotential bonding ties the lift to the pool's bonding system, and bonding jumpers in the pool area are not required to run back to a remote panel, service or electrode.
inspection_fails: Lift set and powered with no bonding jumper to the pool's equipotential grid.
Lift circuit on a plain breaker — no GFCI protection for personnel.
Unlisted residential-grade lift installed at a commercial amenity pool.
Bonding jumper landed only on the branch-circuit equipment ground and never tied into the pool bonding system.

sections.title: Article 682 — Natural and Artificially Made Bodies of Water
sections.plain_explanation:
Intro: electrical installations in and around lakes, ponds, and similar natural or artificial bodies of water that are not pools or fountains — floating structures, docks outside Article 555's scope, and equipment near the water's edge. Florida lakefront work lands here; the shock-hazard logic follows Article 680's thinking.

• 682.12: Floating structures can now have splices between the waterline and the datum plane if they're submersion-rated, and replacement connections in that zone must be listed and identified for submersion. sections.title: Article 685 — Integrated Electrical Systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 685 covers integrated electrical systems — unitized segments of an industrial wiring system where an orderly shutdown is necessary to ensure safe operation. It is not a size or voltage class. A system only qualifies when all three conditions in 685.1 are met at the same time:
• An orderly shutdown is required to minimize personnel hazard and equipment damage — killing power suddenly is itself the danger.
• Conditions of maintenance and supervision ensure that qualified persons service the system, and the names of those qualified persons are kept in a permanent record at the office in charge of the installation.
• Effective safeguards acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction are established and maintained.
Where a system qualifies, the article relaxes a few normal rules so a fault alarm can be answered with a planned shutdown instead of a trip:
• 685.10: overcurrent devices critical to the system may be accessible rather than readily accessible, mounted at heights that keep unqualified personnel from operating them.
• 685.12: two-wire dc circuits are permitted to be ungrounded.
• 685.14: control circuits of 150 volts or less from separately derived systems are permitted to be ungrounded where operational continuity is required.
Table 685.3 in 685.3 points to the sections in other articles — 430.44 for motors is one — that carry their own orderly-shutdown provisions.
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only. Sharma's work is houses and small commercial, so this article shows up for us as a reading skill, not an installation method: where a facility's drawings show an integrated electrical system, its orderly-shutdown documentation is part of the electrical record — keep it with the panel directories in the job file, and do not rewire interconnections between systems without the engineer of record. If a service call ever takes a crew into a plant that runs under 685, the first question is who the named qualified persons are; if nobody can produce that record, the system is not being run the way the article requires.
sections.why_it_exists: In a chemical plant, a steel mill, or over a scrap yard, sudden power loss is not the safe state — it is the accident. A lifting electromagnet drops its load, a reaction runs away, molten metal freezes in the wrong place. Article 685 trades the normal accessibility and grounding rules for supervision: alarms announce a fault, and trained people shut the process down in sequence before anyone gets hurt.
sections.exam_trap: The exam trap is "any large industrial service." Article 685 is not about size — a big plant that fails any one of the three 685.1 conditions is wired under the normal rules, readily accessible overcurrent devices and grounded systems included.
inspection_fails: Qualified persons' names missing from the permanent record at the office in charge of the installation (685.1).
Safeguards for the integrated system not established, not maintained, or never accepted by the AHJ (685.1).
Critical overcurrent devices moved down to readily accessible height during a later alteration, defeating the security 685.10 allows.
Interconnections between systems rewired in the field with no engineer of record and no update to the shutdown documentation.

sections.title: Article 690 — Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 690 covers PV systems from the module terminals to the point of connection: how circuit current is figured (690.8), how conductors and overcurrent devices are sized (690.8, 690.9), maximum voltage (690.7), ground-fault and arc-fault protection (690.41(B) and 690.11; the old 690.5 number was deleted in 2020), rapid shutdown on buildings (690.12), disconnects (690.13, 690.15), and the marking that tells the next person — and the fire department — what the system is (690.56). Interconnection to the premises system runs through Article 705: the 120% bus rule lives at 705.12(B)(3)(2) in Chapter 7 and is deliberately not repeated here.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 690.4: New 690.4(G) covers PV that floats on ponds, lakes and reservoirs: the equipment must be identified for floating use, and the wiring method has to handle the array's movement. Floating PV, whether the gear rides on the water itself or mounts to something that floats, must be identified for that use (690.4(G)).
• Article 690: The use of the term "PV output circuit" has been removed throughout
• 690.1: Added new simplified illustrations to Section 690.1 identifying typical PV system dc components and conductors using new or revised definitions.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Ground-fault protection (690.41(B) in 2020; the old 690.5 was deleted)
sections.plain_explanation: PV systems must be provided with ground-fault protection meeting this section: the system detects a ground fault in the DC circuits, interrupts the faulted circuit, and indicates the fault, using equipment listed for PV ground-fault protection. It is the DC-side companion to 690.11's arc-fault protection — ground faults and series arcs are different failures and one device does not cover both.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call, a tripped ground-fault indication inside the inverter is a find-the-fault call, not a reset-and-leave call.

sections.title: Maximum voltage — correct Voc for cold
sections.plain_explanation:
A PV string's voltage is not its nameplate total. Module open-circuit voltage rises as temperature falls, so maximum system voltage is calculated from the sum of the series modules' rated open-circuit voltages corrected to the lowest expected ambient temperature at the site, using a method 690.7(A) allows: the manufacturer's temperature coefficient of Voc from the module listing instructions, or the correction factors of Table 690.7(A) for crystalline and multicrystalline silicon modules. The corrected voltage must not exceed the rated voltage of the connected equipment (inverter input, disconnects, conductors), and maximum PV system voltage for one- and two-family dwellings is limited to 600V.

Table 690.7(A) correction factors (crystalline and multicrystalline silicon modules), by lowest expected ambient temperature:
• 4°C to 0°C — 1.10
• −1°C to −5°C — 1.12
• −6°C to −10°C — 1.14
• −11°C to −15°C — 1.16
• −16°C to −20°C — 1.18
• −21°C to −25°C — 1.20
Florida's lowest expected ambient temperatures usually fall in the 1.02–1.12 rows; use the site's design low (e.g., the ASHRAE extreme annual mean minimum, per the Informational Note) — but the factor is taken from the site's lowest expected temperature, not from the weather on install day. Warmer Table 690.7(A) rows used in central and south Florida: 24 to 20°C — 1.02; 19 to 15°C — 1.04; 14 to 10°C — 1.06; 9 to 5°C — 1.08 (above the 4 to 0°C row at 1.10). 690.7(A)(3): systems with inverter generating capacity of 100 kW or more may use a documented, stamped engineering method — PE design required; flag for Sanjay.
sections.on_the_job: Size the string on the coldest bright morning of the year, not on the day of the install — over-voltage on a frosty sunrise is the failure this section exists to prevent.
sections.figure_idea: Thermometer at dawn beside an array; Voc arrow rising as the temperature falls; 600V dwelling cap marked.

sections.title: Circuit current and conductor sizing
sections.plain_explanation: PV current is figured on the article's own multipliers, not on load estimates. (A) The maximum current for a PV source circuit is the sum of the parallel module short-circuit currents multiplied by 125%. (B) Conductors are then sized at the larger of two numbers: 125% of the (A) current before any temperature correction or adjustment factors, or 100% of the (A) current after those factors are applied. Both checks must be run — either one can govern depending on the rooftop temperature and fill.
sections.on_the_job:
Do the two-step check on paper; hot Florida rooftops make the after-correction figure govern more often than installers expect.

Worked example: two parallel strings of modules with an Isc of 10.4 A each — the maximum current under 690.8(A) is (10.4 + 10.4) × 1.25 = 26 A. The conductors are then sized at the larger of 26 × 1.25 = 32.5 A before temperature correction and adjustment factors, or the 26 A figure after those factors are applied. Run both numbers on the worksheet; the bigger one buys the wire.
sections.figure_idea: Worksheet sketch: parallel Isc sum × 1.25, then the two conductor checks side by side.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection
sections.plain_explanation:
Where overcurrent protection is required for a PV circuit, the device rating is not less than 125% of the maximum current figured under 690.8(A). The section also states the two-condition case in which no overcurrent device is required at all — conductors sized for the full available current and no external source able to backfeed beyond their ampacity. String fusing questions are answered by applying those conditions, not by habit.

sections.title: Arc-fault circuit protection (DC)
sections.plain_explanation: PV systems with DC circuits operating at 80V dc or greater between any two conductors must be protected by a listed PV arc-fault circuit interrupter, or other listed system components providing equivalent protection. The protection must detect and interrupt arcing faults caused by a failure in the intended continuity of a conductor, connection, module, or other component in the PV DC circuits. Exception: systems not installed on or in buildings, with the DC circuits in metallic raceways or metal-clad cables, in enclosed metallic cable trays, or underground.
sections.on_the_job: Loose MC4-style connections are the classic series-arc source — connector discipline on the roof is what keeps this protection from ever having to work.

sections.title: Rapid shutdown of PV systems on buildings
sections.plain_explanation:
Rapid shutdown controls PV conductors on and in buildings to protect firefighters. The array boundary is 1 ft from the array in all directions. Outside the boundary — and for conductors more than 3 ft from the point of entry into the building — controlled conductors must be limited to not more than 30V within 30 seconds of initiation. Inside the boundary, the installation must use one of the section's paths: a listed PV hazard control system (PVHCS, UL 3741), or conductors limited to not more than 80V within 30 seconds, or an array with no exposed wiring methods or conductive parts and installed not less than 8 ft from exposed grounded conductive parts. The v1 lookup L-093 covers this section and is linked, not rewritten.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 690.12: Carports, parking shades and other open detached structures can now carry PV without rapid shutdown. The third inside-array option is gone, and the building label moved into 690.12(D). New Exception No. 2: PV on nonenclosed detached structures, such as carports, parking shade structures and solar trellises, skips rapid shutdown.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Rapid shutdown initiation device
sections.plain_explanation: The initiation device must be readily accessible, must clearly indicate whether it is in the off (shutdown initiated) or on position, and may be the service disconnect, the PV system disconnect, or another listed switch. For one- and two-family dwellings, the initiation device must be located at a readily accessible location outside the building — the fire crew does not enter the house to shut the array down.
sections.on_the_job: On dwelling jobs, walk out front and find the initiation point the way a firefighter would — if you can't, neither can they.

sections.title: PV system disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation:
Means shall be provided to disconnect the PV system from all wiring systems — the utility power system, any energy storage system, and the utilization equipment and its premises wiring. The disconnecting means has to pass three checks:
• Be installed at a readily accessible location (690.13(A)) — reachable quickly, without a ladder, a locked room, or a trip through the building.
• Plainly indicate whether it is in the open (off) or closed (on) position (690.13(B)).
• Be permanently marked "PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT" (690.13(B)) — a real marking that survives the weather, not tape or marker.
Where all the terminals of the disconnect can still be energized with the switch open — the array side stays live in sunlight — a warning sign goes on or next to the disconnect. Where the PV disconnect is not at the service equipment, the directory and plaque rules of 690.56 point back to where it is, so every source at the building can be found from the service.
sections.on_the_job: Rooftop PV on a Florida house: the inverter sits on the garage wall and the crew lands the PV system disconnect outside, beside the Siemens meter-main, where it is readily accessible from grade. It is a real switch that shows OPEN and ON, permanently marked PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT. Because it is grouped at the service, the 690.56 plaque at the same spot names it with the building's other sources. The homeowner is told plainly: the switch kills the connection, but the panels and their leads stay live in daylight.
sections.why_it_exists: A PV array makes power whenever light hits it, so opening the utility breaker does not make the solar side safe. The disconnect is the one place a firefighter, a utility crew, or the next electrician can separate the PV system from every other wiring system and know it is open. If it is hidden, unmarked, or ambiguous about its position, somebody works on conductors they believe are dead that are not.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering that the rapid shutdown switch, or the inverter's own control, satisfies 690.13. Rapid shutdown (690.12) limits conductor voltage for firefighters; it is not the PV system disconnecting means. 690.13 wants a disconnecting means that separates the PV system from all wiring systems, sits where it is readily accessible, plainly shows open or closed, and is permanently marked PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT.
inspection_fails: PV disconnect inside the attic or behind a locked gate — not readily accessible (690.13(A)).
Disconnect marked with tape or a marker — the marking is not permanent (690.13(B)).
Switch gives no plain indication of open versus closed position (690.13(B)).
PV disconnect remote from the service, with no directory or plaque at the service equipment pointing to it (690.56).

sections.title: Disconnection of PV equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
690.15 is about isolating one piece of PV equipment — an inverter, a charge controller, a dc-to-dc converter — so it can be serviced or replaced with every source cut off. The disconnecting means must open all ungrounded conductors from all sources:
• The array side. The modules make power whenever there is light; opening the ac side does nothing to the dc input.
• The utility side. The grid backfeeds the inverter's ac terminals until its ac disconnect is opened.
• The storage side, on hybrid systems with batteries.
Location (2020): the isolating device or equipment disconnect goes in the equipment, or within sight and within 10 ft of it. Where it sits farther away, it must be capable of being locked in the open position (110.25). An isolating device that is not rated to interrupt the circuit current must be marked "Do Not Disconnect Under Load."
sections.on_the_job: Before opening an inverter, verify both sides are dead — the array makes power whenever the sun is up. On a Florida rooftop hybrid job that is three checks, not two: open the dc disconnect at the inverter and meter the array input, open the ac disconnect and meter the output, and open the battery disconnect on the storage side. The 690.15 disconnects sit at the inverter — within sight and within 10 ft — so the tech who opened them can see them from the equipment while the cover is off.

sections.why_it_exists: PV equipment is fed from directions that do not behave like a normal circuit. There is no switch on the sun: an inverter whose ac side is off still has live dc at its terminals in full daylight, and a hybrid inverter adds a battery that never sleeps. This section exists so the person opening the equipment can put every one of those sources behind an open, visible disconnect first.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'the PV system disconnect is off, so the inverter is safe to open.' The 690.13 system disconnect separates the system from the building and the grid; it does nothing about the array wired straight into the inverter's dc terminals. Rapid shutdown (690.12) is the other wrong answer — it limits conductor voltage for firefighters, it does not isolate equipment for service. 690.15 isolation is per piece of equipment, from every source.

sections.title: Wiring methods — PV source and output circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
690.31 is where solar wiring stops being ordinary branch-circuit wiring. Exposed single-conductor PV source-circuit wiring is a listed PV cable type (Type PV wire, or USE-2 where the section permits it) — conductors built and marked for sunlight, heat, and rooftop duty, not THHN pulled out of a raceway and left in the sun. Rooftop conductors also live in the hottest part of the job, which is why the temperature rules of Chapter 3 ride along. Where inside a building, PV system DC circuits over 30V or 8A must be in metal raceways, in Type MC cable that complies with 250.118(10), or in metal enclosures, from the point of penetration into the building to the first readily accessible disconnecting means (690.31(D)) — so a dc fault inside a wall is contained in metal. The rule applies inside buildings, not to runs on the building. Module interconnects, home runs, and the inverter output each follow the part of the section written for them — read the subsection for the run in front of you.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 690.31(B): Section 690.31(B) was revised and a new list item (1), Conductors of Different Systems, was added while the previous text in that location was moved to list item (2), Identification. The text revisions provide conditions where PV dc circuits and inverter output circuits can now be installed in the same junction box, pull box or wireway provided they are identified, grouped, and separated in accordance with 690.31 (B)(2) and (B)(3).
• 690.31(B)(1): Exception revised to permit the dc and ac conductors of a PV system to be located within the same enclosure where all the conductors are insulated for the highest voltage present and grouped appropriately.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

Loose THHN or cable not listed for the exposure, lying on a Florida roof, is a failed inspection and a cooked conductor.

sections.title: Grounding electrode system — PV ties into the building system
sections.plain_explanation: A PV installation does not get its own separate grounding world. 690.47 ties the array's equipment grounding and any dc grounding electrode conductor into the building's grounding electrode system, so the array, the service, and everything else bonded in the building sit at the same potential. An additional electrode at the array — a ground rod driven by the racking — is permitted, but it supplements the system: it is an auxiliary electrode under 690.47(B) and 250.54. It may connect directly to the array frame or structure, and it does not have to be bonded to the building GES, because the bonding path back to the service is the array's equipment grounding conductor (Part VII of Article 250). The earth is never the fault-current path., and it never replaces that connection. A rod in the dirt by the array with no bond back to the service is a decoration, not a grounding electrode system. A rod with no EGC path back to the service is not compliant: the array equipment grounding conductors connect to the building's grounding electrode system per 690.47(A).
sections.on_the_job: Ground-mount or roof array: bond the racking and equipment back to the house grounding electrode system, and if the design adds a rod at the array, bond that rod in too. The inspector's question is always the same — show me the path back to the service ground.

sections.title: Marking — plaques, directories, and the rapid shutdown label
sections.plain_explanation:
PV systems carry permanent plaques and directories: a stand-alone system follows the directory rule of 710.10, and a system interconnected with another source follows 705.10, so the sources at a building can be found from the service equipment. Two rapid-shutdown labels apply: a permanent label on or within 3 ft of the service disconnecting means states that the system is equipped with rapid shutdown and carries the 690.56(C) diagram with the switch locations; and a reflective label on or within 3 ft of the rapid shutdown initiation device reads RAPID SHUTDOWN SWITCH FOR SOLAR PV SYSTEM, in capital letters at least 3/8 in. high, white on a red background (690.56(C)(2)). Marking is not paperwork; it is the part of the system the fire department uses.

sections.title: Article 691 — Large-Scale Photovoltaic (PV) Electric Supply Stations
sections.plain_explanation: Intro: utility-scale PV plants of 5 MW and up — engineered installations with their own access, fencing, and documentation rules. Added in the 2017 edition, not new in 2020. Sharma does not build these; recognize the article so a plant job is never priced from residential 690 habits.
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only: a plant of 5 MW and up is an engineered, fenced, access-controlled installation with its own documentation rules. If a developer asks Sharma to 'hook up' a solar field, the conversation starts with the plant's engineered drawings — never with residential 690 habits.

sections.title: Article 692 — Fuel Cell Systems
sections.plain_explanation: Intro: fuel cell power systems — output circuits, disconnects, and interconnection of a chemical generator that runs whenever fuel is present. Specialty work; the disconnect and marking pages matter when one appears on a commercial job.
sections.on_the_job: A fuel cell keeps making power for as long as fuel reaches it — treat its output as a live source until the fuel supply is shut off and the unit is isolated the way its listing directs. Confirm the disconnect and the interconnection point from the manufacturer's documents before touching the output circuit.

sections.title: Article 694 — Wind Electric Systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 694 covers small wind electric systems: the turbine, its tower, and the generators, alternators, inverters, and controllers that turn wind into premises power, interconnected with the utility or standing alone, with or without battery storage. The article's size line is per turbine — each individual wind turbine must be rated 100 kW or less. Utility-scale machines live under utility rules, not this article.
• The turbine itself is part of the electrical system (694.2 counts the tower, nacelle, and turbine output circuit as system parts), and 694.7 requires the wind electric system to be listed.
• 694.10: on one- and two-family dwellings, the wind turbine output circuit is limited to 600 volts maximum.
• 694.12: system currents are treated as continuous — conductors are sized at not less than 125 percent of the maximum circuit current.
• 694.15: turbine output circuits, inverter output circuits, and storage conductors get overcurrent protection under Article 240, sized on the same 125 percent basis.
• 694.20: a disconnecting means for the system must be readily accessible and open all ungrounded conductors.
• An interactive system interconnects under 694.60 and 694.62, which send you to Article 705, using inverters listed and identified as interactive.
sections.on_the_job: Recognition only: a small wind system's disconnects, grounding, and tower work follow the turbine manufacturer's listing and this article. Sharma's likely piece is the supply-side connection — confirm the turbine's own disconnect and tower grounding are in the turbine installer's scope before pricing ours. If a quote ever does land, the sizing habit to bring is the 125 percent rule: a turbine whose maximum output current is 40 A needs conductors sized for at least 50 A before any temperature or fill adjustment.
sections.why_it_exists: You cannot switch off the wind. A turbine keeps generating as long as the rotor turns, and an unloaded turbine in a gust can overspeed and tear itself apart — so the article builds safety out of listing, continuous-duty sizing, and a real disconnect, instead of pretending the source can be shut down like a utility feed.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing wind circuits like ordinary loads. Wind output is continuous by rule — 694.12 sizes conductors at 125 percent of the maximum circuit current, not the nameplate's fair-weather rating, and the disconnect still has to open every ungrounded conductor.
inspection_fails: Turbine output conductors sized at 100 percent of maximum circuit current instead of 125 percent (694.12).
AC-only breaker protecting a dc turbine output circuit — the device must be rated for the circuit it protects (694.15).
No readily accessible disconnecting means, or one that leaves an ungrounded conductor closed (694.20).
Grid used as the only overspeed protection — an interconnected grid is not an adequate alternate diversion load (694.7).
Unlisted turbine system installed as a field-assembled kit (694.7).

sections.title: Article 695 — Fire Pumps
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 695 exists for one reason: the fire pump must run, even at the cost of the equipment itself. Everything in it runs backward from ordinary motor practice — sources are chosen for reliability above all (695.3), overcurrent devices are sized to carry locked-rotor current indefinitely rather than to trip (695.4), and disconnects are arranged so the pump cannot be casually shut off. Recognition level is the right depth for Sharma: this is engineered, AHJ-scrutinized work, and the pages here cover what to recognize and what never to improvise. The article does not apply to sprinkler-system pumps at one- and two-family dwellings, and pressure-maintenance (jockey) pumps sit outside its scope as pumps — though their current counts in the 695.3 source sizing.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 695.1: Article 695 now plainly excludes fire suppression water pumps in one- and two-family homes, so a house sprinkler pump isn't treated as a fire pump. New item (4) in 695.1(B) takes fire suppression water pumps in one- and two-family homes out of Article 695.
• 695.15: Diesel-driven fire pumps no longer need a surge-protective device at the controller. Electric fire pumps still do. New exception: a diesel-driven fire pump doesn't need a surge-protective device (SPD) at its controller.
• 695.6: Every fitting on the controller-to-motor wiring for a fire pump now needs a wet-location listing. The wiring methods and motor connection rules carried over. New 695.6(D)(2): every fitting on the controller-to-motor run has to be listed for wet locations.

sections.title: Power sources — reliable, and sized for locked rotor
sections.plain_explanation: The fire pump supply must come from a reliable source, and the source is sized to carry the locked-rotor current of the fire pump motor(s) plus the pressure-maintenance pump motors, plus 100% of the accessory equipment load — locked rotor, not full load, is the design event. Permitted arrangements include a separate utility service arranged remote from the normal service, a tap ahead of (but not within the enclosure of) the normal service disconnect, and an on-site standby generator protected against fire damage. Where transfer equipment is used, it sits in the fire pump room (695.3(F)). Phase converters are not permitted as the supply (695.3(I)).
sections.on_the_job: Recognize the tap-ahead-of-the-main arrangement when you see it on existing work — it is deliberate, not a violation.
sections.figure_idea: One-line: normal service and fire pump tap ahead of the main, generator as second source.

sections.title: Continuity of power — protection that refuses to trip
sections.plain_explanation: Continuity rules invert ordinary practice. A single disconnecting means is permitted where it is listed for fire pump service together with the controller (or transfer switch) it feeds. Its overcurrent device is selected to carry, indefinitely, the sum of the locked-rotor currents of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motors plus the full accessory load, and it must be listed for fire pump use. The disconnect must be lockable in the closed position — the opposite of the elevator rule — and is identified with permanently marked letters not less than 1 in. high as a fire pump disconnect. No ground-fault protection of equipment is applied to the fire pump circuit: anything that can shut the pump down on a fault that isn't a short circuit is designed out.
sections.on_the_job: Field recognition: a fire pump disconnect that looks 'oversized' and is locked ON is correct. Never 'fix' one to ordinary motor sizing.
sections.figure_idea: Disconnect placard: 'FIRE PUMP DISCONNECT' in 1 in. letters, lock through the closed-position hasp.

sections.title: Transformers — dedicated and oversized
sections.plain_explanation: Transformers between the system supply and the fire pump controller are sized at not less than 125% of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motor loads plus 100% of the fire-pump accessory equipment they supply (695.5(B)). 'Dedicated' is not absolute: only a feeder-source transformer covered by 695.5(C) may also supply loads not directly associated with the fire pump system. Primary overcurrent protection is sized to carry indefinitely the sum of the locked-rotor currents of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motors plus the full-load current of the accessory equipment, and no secondary OCPD is permitted (695.5(B)) — the transformer protection is not allowed to become the weak link that stops the pump.
sections.on_the_job: Field check: a transformer supplying a fire pump installation serves that installation — only a 695.5(C) feeder-source transformer may also carry other loads. If existing work shows building loads tapped off a fire pump transformer, report it — do not add Sharma loads to it, and do not 'correct' its protection to ordinary 450.3 sizing.

sections.title: Voltage drop — 15% starting, 5% running
sections.plain_explanation:
One of the NEC's few mandatory voltage-drop rules, and it is a calculation rule: (A) starting — the voltage at the controller's line terminals must not drop more than 15% below normal (controller-rated) voltage under motor starting conditions; (B) running — the voltage at the controller's load terminals must not drop more than 5% below the motor's voltage rating when the motor operates at 115% of its full-load current. Conductors under 695.6(B) must satisfy both their ampacity floor and these limits.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 695.7: Fire pump voltage drop was rebuilt around the fire pump installation standard's limits: 15 percent starting, 5 percent running, with two starting carve-outs that need a proven generator start. Starting (695.7(A)): the controller's line terminals must hold at least 85 percent of the controller's rated voltage.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
